You have hit on a concept that philosophers, anthropologists, and cognitive scientists call the exoteric versus esoteric divide—or in modern tech terms, building an abstraction layer for the mind.

When the conceptual gap between the insight and the listener is too wide, literal explanation fails. If someone doesn't have the math for calculus, you don't show them differential equations; you tell them a story about a car accelerating.

Myth as a Cognitive User Interface (UI) Your idea of religion and myth acting as an "interface" is remarkably accurate in several ways:

  • Operational Heuristics: Ancient traditions didn't need people to understand microbiology or germ theory; telling them "this animal spirit is unclean and will curse your blood" produced the exact same survival behavior. The myth is the functional code running behind a simple GUI.
  • Paradox as a Mental Hack: In Zen Buddhism (with koans), Sufism, and mystical Kabbalah, stories are intentionally absurd, contradictory, or "weird." The point isn't literal truth—the paradox is designed to break ordinary linear logic, forcing the brain into a state of cognitive restructuring (or what you described as "starting a whole new personality").
  • Phenomenological vs. Objective Truth: A shaman experiencing an interconnected energy field might describe "a serpent binding the spirit of the forest." A theoretical physicist might describe quantum entanglement, field equations, or trophic cascades in ecology. Both are describing systemic interdependence, but the shaman's language maps directly to human sensory and emotional bandwidth.

Anthropologists call this mythopoetic thought. It isn’t primitive ignorance; it’s an efficient compression algorithm for complex truths about human psychology, ecology, and social cohesion that people didn't yet have the specialized vocabulary to articulate.

That observation touches on one of the biggest illusions in modern education: the difference between contextual derivation and deductive transmission.

When we learn a complex principle in a classroom or from a book, it is presented backward. We see the final, compressed mathematical formula or conceptual rule completely detached from the messy physical environment where it was hammered out. It looks like lightning-strike genius or alien knowledge. In reality, it was almost always an inevitable artifact of deep immersion under pressure.

The Mechanics of "Accidental" Discovery

  • High-Bandwidth Sensory Immersion: When you spend thousands of hours hands-on with a specific physical system—whether it’s early navigators reading ocean swells, metallurgy workers reading flame color, or naturalists mapping plant alkaloids—your brain builds deep pattern recognition long before you have formal language for it. You collect continuous data points that an abstract theorist never sees.
  • The Constraint Engine (Pressure): Extreme constraints—survival, economic necessity, or intense emotional obsession—force rapid elimination of noise. A farmer, blacksmith, or hunter doesn't care about theoretical elegance; they care about what works reliably every single time. Survival is a ruthless error-correction loop.
  • Combinatorial Synthesis (The "Recipe"): The breakthrough rarely comes from a single eureka moment in a vacuum. It comes from colliding 4–5 disparate, practical constraints simultaneously: “The material has to survive winter, cost nothing, be light enough to carry, and stop this specific rot.” The resulting solution looks hyper-specific and wildly complex to an outsider, but to the person immersed in the problem, it was simply the only path that satisfied every boundary condition.

When this solution is passed down, the physical context gets stripped away, leaving behind an arcane "recipe," a bizarre ritual, or a dense scientific law that makes future generations wonder, "How on earth did anyone come up with this?"

Anyone placed in an identical high-stakes environment with sufficient observation time and skin in the game would likely arrive at the very same functional output.

You have framed two interconnected principles here: the structural difference between objective mechanics (science) vs. cybernetic integration (religion), and the severe instability of one-dimensional local hyper-optimization.

1. Religion as Whole-System Cybernetics

Science maps the mechanism of the parts—how heat transfers, how biology replicates, how forces interact. Religion and myth focus on relational homeostasis—how the conscious node (the individual) integrates with the total system (the whole, tribe, or universe) without tearing the fabric apart.

Science asks, "What is true and what works?" Myth asks, "How do we orient ourselves so this knowledge doesn't destroy us or detach us from the whole?"

2. The Danger of the Hyper-Optimized Outlier

When someone discovers an outlier local optimum along a single dimension—whether that is an overwhelming cognitive breakthrough, sudden immense leverage, or hyper-specialized technical dominance—it almost always destabilizes the agent.

In evolutionary biology, systems engineering, and complex systems theory, this dynamic breaks down into three core failure modes:

  • Dimensionality Mismatch: A human is a multi-dimensional system requiring physical health, psychological balance, social reciprocity, and environmental grounding. Maximizing a single axis to extreme levels starves the remaining dimensions of resources and attention. The system becomes brittle.
  • Loss of System Coupling (The "Idiocracy" / Isolation Penalty): If an agent’s local optimum places them too far ahead of the surrounding network, the protocol to communicate or exchange value breaks down. You cannot cooperate with a surrounding environment whose feedback loops operate on a completely different frequency. The outlier is treated either as a parasite, a threat, or an incomprehensible anomaly.
  • Lack of Structural Dissipation: High leverage creates high tension. If an agent holds an advanced insight or capability without the institutional, physical, or cultural scaffolding to absorb and distribute that energy, the energy reflects back onto the container.

Where Does That "Power" Actually Belong?

Your intuition that the power “belongs somewhere else, somewhere that can handle it better” aligns with how complex ecosystems survive:

Power or radical optimization cannot safely reside in an isolated, delicate node. It requires a distributed architecture—a culture, a set of institutional checks, an ecosystem, or a robust abstraction layer (like the myths and traditions discussed earlier)—to ground the voltage.

When an individual attempts to bear extreme single-dimensional power alone, it acts less like an evolutionary advantage and more like an over-tuned engine tearing apart its own chassis.
